passage:
"Ujjwal, I have to tell you that the project is closing," said Mridul in the small cabin. "Your role ends at the end of this month. I'm sorry."
"Okay," said Ujjwal.
"Do you have any questions?"
"No. Okay."
"Take your time to absorb it."
"It's fine. Thanks for telling me."
Ujjwal walked back to the desk, finished the email that was half-written, went for lunch, ate all of it. Around six, in the parking lot, Ujjwal's hand froze on the key. Then the whole thing arrived at once, and Ujjwal sat on the bike and cried, phone lighting up with messages.

qa.q: What did Mridul tell Ujjwal in the cabin?
qa.a: That the project is closing and Ujjwal's role ends at the end of the month.

qa.q: What did Ujjwal's flat "Okay" suggest about how Ujjwal felt?
qa.a: Shock. The calm was on the surface, and the real reaction came hours later, in the parking lot.

qa.q: What could someone close to Ujjwal do that evening?
qa.a: Check in kindly, listen without hurrying to solutions, and if the distress keeps going, suggest talking to someone trained to help.

qa.q: How might Mridul have felt delivering the news?
qa.a: Uneasy and sorry, and likely to have taken Ujjwal's calm as a sign of coping, though the reaction was only delayed.

grounding: A person told about a layoff goes flat and says okay, and the real reaction arrives hours later.

passage: My name is Sachin. My sister Bhavna called me on a Tuesday to say that the reports had come, and Papa had been given a serious diagnosis. She spoke quickly, and I said, "Okay. Okay. Thanks for telling me." My voice was steady, so steady she asked if I was still there. I said yes, I was making tea. I finished the tea, answered two emails and went to a meeting. Nothing hurt. That felt strange. Around midnight, standing at the window, I felt it hit, like a wave that had been waiting behind the calm. I called Bhavna back, and she picked up on the first ring.

qa.q: What did Bhavna say when she called on Tuesday?
qa.a: That the reports had come and Papa had been given a serious diagnosis.

qa.q: What did Sachin's steady "Okay" suggest about how Sachin really felt, looking back?
qa.a: Shock. Sachin felt nothing at first and the real feeling arrived near midnight like a wave waiting behind the calm.

qa.q: What was the turning point after the wave hit?
qa.a: Sachin called Bhavna back, so the feeling was shared and not carried alone; talking to the family doctor or a counsellor could help if it stays heavy.

qa.q: How might Bhavna have felt when Sachin answered so steadily?
qa.a: Puzzled or worried, since Bhavna asked whether Sachin was still there, and relieved to be called back and picked up on the first ring.

grounding: A person told about a diagnosis in the family goes flat and says okay, and the real reaction comes hours later.

passage:
"Uday, you said 'okay' when they told you about the layoffs, and now you look like a stone," said Zubin dadaji, pouring tea. "Let me tell you about my first layoff. I was twenty-five, at the textile mill. The manager called twenty of us in, read out our names, and said the mill was closing a section. Everyone around me shouted. I just said, 'Okay.' I walked home, ate dinner, even joked with your grandmother.
Two days later, I was on the bus and saw the mill gate through the window. And I started crying, right there, in front of strangers. I couldn't stop.
So don't worry if you feel nothing today. Shock looks like calm. The real feelings come later. When they come, call me."

qa.q: How many people did the manager call in?
qa.a: Twenty.

qa.q: How did young Zubin feel on the day of the layoff?
qa.a: He felt numb and flat, saying 'Okay' and even joking at dinner.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Zubin dadaji's story?
qa.a: Seeing the mill gate from the bus two days later, when the real feelings arrived and he cried.

qa.q: How might Zubin dadaji's wife have seen his calm that first night?
qa.a: She might have been surprised or worried, sensing his calm was shock rather than peace.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling how he went flat after a layoff, with the real reaction arriving days later.

passage: Maria's phone rang in the middle of the biggest deadline of the quarter. It was her brother. Their father's scans had come back; the doctors had found a tumour. Maria said, "Okay. Okay. Thanks for telling me. I'll call you tonight." She hung up and went back to her spreadsheet. Arohi, at the next desk, noticed. Maria's voice had been flat, and her face showed nothing. She typed steadily for two hours. "Are you okay?" Arohi asked. "Yes, fine. Just family stuff." Arohi didn't push, but she stayed near and made Maria a cup of tea. At home that night, Maria sat down to eat and couldn't lift the spoon. She started shaking, then sobbing. She called Arohi at ten. Arohi answered on the first ring and stayed on the phone for an hour.

qa.q: What did the doctors find?
qa.a: A tumour.

qa.q: What was Maria feeling during the two hours she typed steadily?
qa.a: She was in shock and numb, her flat voice and blank face hiding what she'd heard.

qa.q: How did Arohi support Maria well?
qa.a: She noticed the flatness, didn't push, stayed near with tea, and answered right away when Maria called that night.

qa.q: How might Maria's brother have felt hearing her calm 'Okay'?
qa.a: He might have been surprised or worried that she didn't react more.

grounding: Shows a person receiving hard family news who goes flat and says okay, with the real reaction arriving hours later.

passage: At the Salt Lake office in Kolkata, Dilnaz was called into a meeting room and told her whole team was being laid off at the end of the month. She said, "Okay. I understand." She packed up at five like any other day. On the bus, her friend Kunal called. "Are you alright? I heard." "I'm fine. It's fine." He didn't believe her voice. That evening she cooked dinner, watched a show, went to sleep. The next morning, at the tea stall outside the office, the vendor asked cheerfully, "Same as always, didi?" and Dilnaz burst into tears. She called Kunal. He left work early and met her at the lake. They walked for an hour. "I didn't feel anything yesterday," she said. "I thought something was wrong with me." Kunal said, "It was shock. It just arrived today."

qa.q: When would Dilnaz's team be laid off?
qa.a: At the end of the month.

qa.q: How did Dilnaz feel on the day of the news?
qa.a: She felt numb and flat, saying 'Okay' and going through the evening as usual.

qa.q: What did Kunal do that helped?
qa.a: He called, noticed her voice didn't match her words, and left work early to walk with her when she broke down.

qa.q: What was it like for the tea vendor when Dilnaz burst into tears?
qa.a: The vendor was probably surprised and unsure, since the greeting was cheerful and ordinary.

grounding: Shows a person told about a layoff who goes flat and says okay, with the real reaction arriving the next day.

passage:
"Minakshi, please sit. I'll be direct. The company is closing the Pune design team. Your role ends on the thirtieth."
"Okay."
"You'll get two months' pay, and HR will help with references."
"Okay."
Jagdish paused. "Do you have any questions?"
"No. That's fine. Should I finish the Mehra deck today?"
"You... don't have to."
"I'll finish it."
She walked back to her desk and finished the deck. She even replied to a joke in the team chat.
At eleven that night, brushing her teeth, Minakshi sat down on the bathroom floor and cried for a long time. The next morning she messaged Jagdish: "I think I do have questions now."

qa.q: When does Minakshi's role end?
qa.a: Her role ends on the thirtieth.

qa.q: Why did Minakshi keep saying "Okay" and offer to finish the deck?
qa.a: She was in shock, numb and flat, so the news had not really landed yet; it looked like calm but wasn't.

qa.q: How could Jagdish help after such a flat reaction?
qa.a: He could check in the next day and say questions are welcome at any time, since the real reaction may come later.

qa.q: How might Jagdish have read Minakshi's calm in the meeting?
qa.a: He may have been puzzled or even relieved, thinking she took it well, without seeing the shock underneath.

grounding: Shows a young professional going flat and saying okay on hearing of a layoff, with the real reaction arriving hours later.
